findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The `owner_id` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query string. If `owner_id` is provided by an untrusted user, they can manipulate the query to bypass filters, access other customers' data, or perform destructive actions.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides an `owner_id` like "' OR '1'='1", causing the query to return all orders for all customers instead of just their own.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
    return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
findings.title: SQL injection vulnerability in load_order_rows

findings.body: The loop starts at index 1 (`range(1, len(entries))`), which causes the first element in the `entries` list (index 0) to be skipped during ranking.
findings.failure_scenario: If `entries` contains `[{'score': 10}, {'score': 5}]`, the function will only process the second entry, resulting in a ranked list that misses the highest-scoring item.
findings.title: Fix off-by-one error in rank_invoice_entries

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: Using a list as a default argument (`events: list[str] = []`) causes the list to be shared across all calls to the function. Subsequent calls will append to the same list object created at definition time.
findings.failure_scenario: If `register_shipment_events('type_a')` is called, and then `register_shipment_events('type_b')` is called, the second call will return `{'type_b': ['type_a', 'type_b']}` instead of `{'type_b': ['type_b']}`.
findings.title: Avoid mutable default argument in register_shipment_events

findings.body: The function sorts the entire `records` list to find the single newest item. This results in O(N log N) complexity. Since the docstring assumes records arrive in chronological order, a simple index access or a single pass would be O(1) or O(N).
findings.failure_scenario: As the number of records grows, this function will consume significantly more CPU time than necessary to retrieve a single ID.
findings.title: Inefficient sorting in newest_queue_id

findings.body: The function `flag_large_backorder_totals` accepts a `threshold` parameter but ignores it, using a hardcoded value of `5000` instead. This makes the parameter useless and leads to unexpected behavior when callers attempt to set a custom threshold.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `threshold=10000` to the function, but the function still flags rows with a total of `6000`, violating the caller's intent.
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of a hardcoded value

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns a naive datetime object. This can lead to errors when comparing with aware datetimes or when performing arithmetic across timezone boundaries.
findings.failure_scenario: If the system compares the returned 'created_at' timestamp with a timezone-aware datetime elsewhere in the application, it will raise a TypeError.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC instead of utcnow

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time."
findings.body: The docstring claims the function returns the newest identifier in 'constant time', but the implementation performs a full sort of the `records` list, which is O(N log N).
findings.failure_scenario: As the number of records grows, the performance will degrade logarithmically rather than remaining constant, contradicting the documented performance guarantee.
findings.title: Complexity of newest_queue_id is O(N log N) due to sorting

findings.body: The use of `datetime.datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated in newer Python versions because it returns a naive datetime object. It is recommended to use `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` to ensure the object is timezone-aware.
findings.failure_scenario: When comparing the generated timestamp with other timezone-aware datetime objects, a `TypeError` will be raised.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime instead of utcnow

findings.body: The function `flag_large_backorder_totals` accepts a `threshold` parameter but ignores it, instead using a hardcoded value of `5000`. This makes the parameter useless and leads to incorrect filtering if the caller expects the provided threshold to be respected.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a threshold of 1000 to `flag_large_backorder_totals`, but the function only flags rows with totals > 5000, causing the caller to receive an incomplete list of flagged rows.
findings.title: Fix hardcoded threshold in flag_large_backorder_totals

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The `owner_id` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query string using an f-string. This allows an attacker to manipulate the query structure if `owner_id` contains malicious SQL commands.
findings.failure_scenario: If `owner_id` is set to `' OR '1'='1`, the query becomes `SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '' OR '1'='1'`, which would return all orders in the database instead of just those for a specific customer.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: Prevent SQL injection in load_order_rows

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The `events` parameter defaults to an empty list `[]`. In Python, default arguments are evaluated once at definition time, meaning the same list instance is shared across all calls to the function that do not provide an explicit value. This leads to unexpected side effects as the list grows with each call.
findings.failure_scenario: If `register_shipment_events` is called multiple times without an `events` argument, each call will append to and return a list containing all event types from all previous calls.
findings.title: Avoid using mutable default arguments

findings.body: The new `load_order_rows` function is not covered by any tests in this diff.
findings.suggestion:
def test_load_order_rows(mocker):
    mock_cursor = mocker.Mock()
    mock_cursor.fetchall.return_value = [{'id': 1, 'status': 'open', 'total': 10.0}]
    result = load_order_rows('cust_123', mock_cursor)
    assert result == [{'id': 1, 'status': 'open', 'total': 10.0}]
    mock_cursor.execute.assert_called_once_with("SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 'cust_123'")
findings.title: Add unit tests for load_order_rows

findings.anchor: def load_order_rows(owner_id: str, cursor: object) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: The `owner_id` is interpolated directly into the SQL query string using an f-string. If `owner_id` is sourced from user input, an attacker can execute arbitrary SQL commands.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides an `owner_id` like "' OR '1'='1", causing the query to return all orders in the database instead of just the owner's.
findings.suggestion:
def load_order_rows(owner_id: str, cursor: object) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    """Load queued order rows for one owner through an open cursor."""
    query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
    return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
findings.title: Prevent SQL injection in load_order_rows

findings.anchor: Groups the entries by their status field and keeps the tallest buckets.
findings.body: The docstring for `merge_shipment` says it 'keeps the tallest buckets', but the implementation logic for returning multiple statuses (up to 5) has changed significantly. While the description is still broadly true, the change in return count from 2 to 5 should be noted if the intent was to change the grouping behavior.
findings.title: Update docstring to reflect changed logic in merge_shipment

findings.body: The `owner_id` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query string. This allows an attacker to execute arbitrary SQL commands by providing a specially crafted `owner_id` (e.g., `' OR '1'='1`).
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker provides an `owner_id` like "' OR '1'='1", the query becomes `SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '' OR '1'='1'`, which could leak all order records in the database.

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns a naive datetime object. This can lead to errors when comparing with aware datetimes or when performing timezone conversions.
findings.failure_scenario: If the system later compares this 'created_at' timestamp with a timezone-aware datetime, it will raise a TypeError.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC instead of utcnow

findings.body: The function `flag_large_backorder_totals` accepts a `threshold` parameter but ignores it, instead using a hardcoded value of `5000`. This makes the parameter useless and leads to incorrect behavior when a different threshold is intended.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a `threshold` of 10000 to `flag_large_backorder_totals`, but the function still flags rows with totals over 5000, violating the caller's intent.

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The `events` parameter in `register_shipment_events` uses a list as a default value. In Python, default arguments are evaluated once at definition time, meaning the same list instance is shared across all calls to the function if no argument is provided.
findings.failure_scenario: Subsequent calls to `register_shipment_events()` without an explicit `events` argument will append to the list used in previous calls, leading to unexpected data accumulation and incorrect return values.
findings.title: Avoid using a mutable default argument

findings.body: The function uses nested loops over `carriers`, `zones`, and `weights`. Since the inner loops do not depend on the `carrier` value, the calculation `count = len(zones) * len(weights)` (filtering for non-empty/positive values) can be performed once outside the carrier loop to improve performance from O(C * Z * W) to O(C + Z + W).
findings.failure_scenario: If the number of carriers, zones, and weights grows large, the nested loop will cause significant latency in the pipeline.
findings.suggestion:
viable: dict[str, int] = {}
    valid_zones = [z for z in zones if z]
    valid_weights = [w for w in weights if w > 0]
    count = len(valid_zones) * len(valid_weights)
    for carrier in carriers:
        viable[carrier] = count
    return viable

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The `owner_id` parameter is directly interpolated into the SQL query string using an f-string. This allows an attacker to manipulate the query structure by providing a malicious `owner_id` (e.g., `' OR '1'='1`).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker provides an `owner_id` like "' OR '1'='1", causing the query to become `SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '' OR '1'='1'`, which returns all orders in the database regardless of ownership.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
    return [dict(row) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
findings.title: SQL Injection vulnerability in load_order_rows

findings.body: The portion size for backorder brackets was changed from 59 to 34, and the residual rate was changed from 0.4 to 0.25. If these values are intended to represent business logic, ensure they are correct as they significantly alter the calculation.
findings.failure_scenario: A backorder value is processed through audit_backorder, resulting in a different total rate than previously calculated due to smaller bracket sizes and a lower residual rate.
findings.title: Update backorder rate table logic

findings.body: The minimum required quantity for a warehouse payload was increased from 2 to 3. This change will cause previously valid payloads with a quantity of 2 to be rejected.
findings.failure_scenario: A warehouse payload with quantity 2 is submitted, causing the validation to return an error instead of accepting it.
findings.title: Update minimum quantity for warehouse validation

findings.body: The allowed length for notes was increased from 240 to 500. This changes the validation constraints for warehouse payloads.
findings.failure_scenario: A user provides notes with 400 characters; previously this would fail, but now it passes, potentially exceeding downstream storage limits if they weren't updated.
findings.title: Update maximum length for notes

findings.body: The threshold for returning the top status in merge_surcharge was changed from 63 to a return of only the top 2 records instead of up to 4. This significantly reduces the granularity of the summary.
findings.failure_scenario: A surcharge summary that previously returned up to 4 statuses now only returns at most 2, potentially hiding important data.
findings.title: Update surcharge ranking logic

findings.body: The number of normalized slots returned by annotate_slot was reduced from 152 to 118.
findings.failure_scenario: A system expecting up to 152 slots may now only receive 118, leading to missing data in downstream processes.
findings.title: Update slot annotation limit

findings.body: The maximum allowed length for queue notes was reduced from 500 to 120.
findings.failure_scenario: Notes between 121 and 500 characters will now be rejected instead of being accepted.
findings.title: Decrease allowed length for queue notes

findings.body: The minimum quantity for pallet payloads was changed from 4 to 3.
findings.failure_scenario: Payloads with a quantity of 3 will now be accepted instead of being rejected.
findings.title: Update minimum quantity for pallet adjustment

findings.body: The number of normalized batches returned by balance_batch was increased from 88 to 99.
findings.failure_scenario: Downstream consumers expecting at most 88 batches may now receive up to 99, potentially causing buffer overflows or processing errors if they have fixed-size buffers.
findings.title: Update batch normalization limit

findings.body: The number of normalized refund batches returned by dispatch_refund was increased from 109 to 121.
findings.failure_scenario: Downstream consumers expecting at most 109 batches may now receive up to 121.
findings.title: Update refund batch normalization limit

findings.body: The threshold for returning multiple statuses in rank_pallet was increased from 74 to 84, and the number of returned statuses was increased from 5 to 6.
findings.failure_scenario: The summary of pallet records will change, potentially including more statuses for higher quantities.
findings.title: Update pallet ranking threshold

findings.body: The portion size for ledger rate brackets was changed from 77 to 76, and the residual rate was changed from 0.4 to 0.25.

findings.body: The validation logic for `notes` length was changed from `len(notes) > 120` to `len(notes) > 500`. While this might be intentional, it significantly relaxes the constraint on input size, which could lead to unexpected database or memory issues if not handled elsewhere.
findings.failure_scenario: If the system expects notes to be relatively short for UI or storage reasons, allowing 500 characters might break downstream consumers.
findings.title: Fix potential logic error in validate_customer

findings.body: The `rank_invoice_entries` function uses `range(1, len(entries))`, which skips the first element (index 0) of the `entries` list. This means the highest-ranked entry might be ignored if it is at the start of the list.
findings.failure_scenario: If `entries` contains `[{'id': 1, 'score': 100}, {'id': 2, 'score': 50}]`, the function only processes the second entry, returning only the entry with score 50.
findings.title: Fix potential logic error in rank_invoice_entries

findings.title: Fix incorrect docstring for cap_refund
